writingPrompt: Directions: Suppose your university newspaper is inviting submissions on the value of learning a practical skill outside your major. You are now to write an essay for submission. You should explain your view and give an example. You will have 30 minutes to write the essay. You should write at least 120 words but no more than 180 words.
writingReference:
University students should be encouraged to learn a practical skill beyond their main subject. Such learning need not distract them from academic work; with a reasonable schedule, it can make that work more meaningful.
One benefit is the opportunity to approach problems in a different way. An engineering student who learns basic cooking, for example, must adjust a plan to the ingredients and time available. Following a formula is useful, but noticing what is happening matters too. This experience can encourage flexibility rather than blind dependence on instructions.
A second benefit is greater independence. Knowing how to prepare a simple meal or mend a piece of clothing allows students to manage ordinary difficulties themselves. These small successes can build confidence that carries into less familiar situations.
Learning an additional skill is therefore worthwhile, provided that students set realistic goals. The aim is not to become an expert in everything, but to become more capable of handling everyday life.

组织：论点、理由与例证相连，结论有依据；不强求固定段数。
语言：语义清楚、搭配和时态准确，有适度句式变化；不以生僻词数量加分。
字数120—180词；参考范文为一种写法，不是官方赋分模型。

In the past, people often gathered in front of open-air stages during festivals to watch performances, through which young audiences also learned about historical stories. Today, while preserving traditional forms of performance, some opera companies are trying to attract more young people through short videos. Many schools also invite performers into classrooms to introduce students to Chinese opera. Through these efforts, this ancient art is becoming part of modern life in new ways.

matchingTitle: A different view from the old railway line
matchingParagraphs: A

I expected the village railway walk to begin with a story about steam engines. Instead, our guide, Mrs Lin, asked us to look at a row of shallow marks in a stone wall. They had been left by ropes used to pull loaded carts towards the former station, yet we had walked past them on our way from the bus without noticing anything unusual. Her question changed the scale of the visit: the route would not simply take us between impressive buildings, but invite us to read ordinary surfaces.
B

The railway had once carried tea and timber from the surrounding hills. After freight services ended, parts of the track were removed and the station became a storehouse; a proposal to turn the whole line into a cycle route was discussed, but several narrow sections would have required major rebuilding. The walking route that eventually opened retained the older bridges and included short diversions where the original line was unsafe. Its slightly uneven path was part of the experience, though suitable shoes were essential. A few surviving rails were displayed at stopping points rather than used as the walking surface.
C

Although the printed map showed a single continuous route, on the ground it was divided into three loops connected by the village square. Mrs Lin explained that visitors often arrived with very different amounts of time. A family waiting for an afternoon bus could complete the shortest loop, while walkers with a full day could continue into the hills. None of the shorter choices required an awkward return along exactly the same path.
D

Our first stop was the old weighing room. The large scale was still there, but the most revealing object was a notebook beside it, copies of whose pages showed how the amount recorded for the same cart could change after damaged packaging was removed. An elderly former clerk had helped explain the figures. Without his account, the columns would have looked like a dull list of numbers rather than evidence of decisions made during a busy working day.
E

Farther along, a low building contained recordings of former railway workers. Although I initially wished there were more dramatic photographs, a voice soon described the difficulty of hearing a colleague through the noise of unloading. Another speaker remembered the silence after the last train had gone. Neither recording offered a complete history. Together they gave the buildings a human scale that the dates on the information boards could not provide. Visitors could listen through handsets, so several accounts could be heard in the same room without competing with one another.
F

The route crossed a stream beside a recently repaired footbridge. Its new wooden surface looked older than it was because the builders had avoided a bright protective finish. Because this had led some visitors to suppose that the bridge was original, a small notice now explained which parts had been replaced and why. Keeping the appearance of an old structure, Mrs Lin said, should not mean concealing the work that made it safe to cross.
G

At the next junction our group spread out. Several people climbed a short flight of steps for a view of the valley, while others remained on a level path. Although I had worried that choosing the easier way would mean missing an important part of the story, both paths reached the same picnic area, where the main information panels were placed. The climb offered a different view rather than access to essential material denied to everyone else.
H

Lunch was served in the former station kitchen. The menu used vegetables from farms nearby, although the owner was careful about the word local. Since rice, for instance, came from another county and some ingredients were unavailable in winter, she preferred to say where things came from rather than promise that every item had travelled only a few kilometres. The meal was simple, but this explanation made the account of village food more convincing.
I

In the afternoon we passed a workshop where an artist used discarded railway metal. I admired a small bird made from a bent fastening, but the artist pointed to a shelf of objects she would not cut up. Some pieces carried numbers that could help identify where they had been used; before accepting material from the site, she asked the local archive whether it should be kept. Giving old objects a new life did not require treating all of them as equally disposable.
J

Near the tunnel, mobile reception disappeared. The visitor website contained an audio description, but I could not open it. Fortunately, the route booklet included the same essential information and a simple diagram stood at the entrance; Mrs Lin said that the booklet had survived several attempts to replace it entirely with phone-based material. A technology that worked well in the village square did not necessarily work equally well along the whole line.
K

We reached the upper station later than planned because a shower had slowed us down. I assumed that the small exhibition there would already be closed. In fact, its opening hours followed the last returning shuttle rather than the working hours of the village office, an arrangement agreed with the drivers and explained in a notice listing the final departure time. It allowed walkers to look around without having to choose between the exhibition and their journey home. On days without a shuttle, the exhibition used a shorter schedule, clearly printed on the route map.
L

Back in the square, I bought a postcard showing the station before the railway closed. The roofs looked familiar, yet the space between them was full of people and goods rather than visitors carrying cameras. The walk had not restored that vanished activity, nor had it turned the village into a fixed picture of the past. It had given me a way to connect details I could see with lives I could only partly imagine. I left noticing marks on walls that would previously have escaped my attention.

Retailers can advertise free delivery without making delivery cost nothing. Packing, transport and the final journey to a customer's door still require resources. What changes is the way in which those costs are covered. They may be included in product prices, covered by a subscription (订阅) or absorbed by a seller expecting future business.
Consider an imaginary experiment involving two otherwise identical online shops. One advertises a lamp at 80 yuan and adds a delivery charge of 10 yuan. The other offers the same lamp for 90 yuan with delivery included. Buying one lamp costs the same at either shop. Nevertheless, the inclusive offer may feel more attractive because the additional charge interrupts a decision the customer has already begun to regard as complete.
This preference does not mean that customers cannot add. A separate fee can be seen as an obstacle imposed by the seller, whereas an inclusive price simplifies the purchase. However, that convenience becomes questionable when customers must reach a minimum order value. Adding an unnecessary product to qualify for free delivery can produce spending greater than the charge being avoided.
A delivery subscription may nevertheless provide genuine savings. For people making frequent small orders, the arrangement can be economical, provided that product prices are competitive and membership does not encourage additional purchases. An occasional customer faces a different calculation: an annual payment for a service used twice cannot be assessed in the same way as one used every week. Comparing delivery charges alone neglects these differences.
The relevant question is therefore not whether an advertisement contains the word free, but what the consumer would spend on purchases already intended. This requires a comparison of total spending and a realistic account of personal shopping habits. Separately charged delivery is not necessarily the worse arrangement, just as an inclusive price is not automatically deceptive. The presentation of a price deserves attention, but it should not substitute for examining what is actually being purchased.

Trees planted along a city street are often judged by what can be seen above ground. A healthy-looking trunk and a broad crown suggest that the planting has succeeded. Yet the space available beneath the pavement can be just as important to a tree's future as the branches that shade the road.
In a fictional neighbourhood renewal project, planners proposed replacing several small trees with larger ones. Residents welcomed the promise of immediate shade. However, an inspection showed that the original planting holes were surrounded by tightly packed material and underground pipes. A larger tree placed in the same restricted space might look impressive at first without remaining healthy for long.
The project team changed its plan. Instead of increasing the size of every new tree, it joined some planting areas beneath the pavement, allowing roots access to a wider volume of soil. This required coordination with people responsible for water pipes and other services. The work was less visible than lifting a mature tree into place, and it could not be completed everywhere along the street. Where essential services left insufficient room, the designers kept a smaller planting area and selected trees suited to it. This made a uniform appearance less important than choosing a workable arrangement for each location.
Nor did the team assume that more growing space would solve every problem. Different tree species respond differently to heat and water, and newly planted trees still need care while they become established. Residents were asked to report damaged supports or dry planting areas. These observations supplemented professional inspections rather than replacing them.
The revised project illustrates a difficulty in judging public improvements. A photograph taken on opening day favours changes that are immediately visible. The conditions that allow those changes to last may remain hidden. This does not make appearance unimportant: shade and an attractive street are real benefits. It does mean that the success of planting should be assessed over time, including whether the trees remain healthy, rather than solely by their size when the work is announced.
